endorsements.quote: To systematically manage AI risks, health care organizations must develop risk assessment protocols that include risk assessment procedures and methodologies by following industrial standards and frameworks as well as best practices [ 63 ].

Data provenance and authentication metrics can be used to prevent collecting data from untrustworthy sources; detecting and filtering methods can be used to identify and filter poisoned data; and data standardization improves the quality of data collection [ 57 ].
In the model implementation phase, routine verification and validation are key to identifying and controlling AI risks [ 63 ].

unlisted_practices: Establish data collection and generation policies and procedures for generative AI in health care.
Separate clinical and nonclinical data given their differing risks.
Establish metrics and methods to check training data for bias, separately for clinical and nonclinical data.
Ensure data collected from medical sources or generated by GANs reflect the comprehensive breadth of the medical domain to prevent bias.
Build a taxonomy of AI models and their risks to systematically identify and control security and privacy risks by model type.

Develop risk assessment metrics for each of the three life cycle phases of a generative AI project, including confidentiality, integrity, availability, nonrepudiation, authentication, and privacy protection objectives.
Conduct security tests along with social, philosophical, and ethical tests when generative AI is integrated into multiagent systems or medical robotics.
Test generative AI in the specific populations and cultural contexts of use, such as teenage populations or culturally sensitive gesture and face recognition.

screen.reason: This is a viewpoint paper exploring privacy and security challenges of generative AI across its lifecycle and proposing governance/mitigation strategies.
